entries.term: I'd like to start by (doing something)
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to announce the first thing you will do in a talk, lecture or meeting.
entries.usage: Common at the start of talks, lectures and meetings: *I'd like to start by thanking the organizers*; *I'd like to start by showing you a picture*. *By* takes an *-ing* form, while *with* takes a noun (*start with a question*). A short, concrete opening works better than a long list of what you will cover.
entries.pattern: I'd like to start by + -ing; I'd like to start with + noun
examples: **I'd like to start by** thanking the organizers for inviting me to Denver.
**I'd like to start by** showing you a photo of this river taken in 1960.
Before we get into the budget, **I'd like to start by** welcoming our two new team members.

drill.sentence: {{I'd like to start by}} asking you a question: how many hours did you sleep last night?
drill.hint: polite opening for the first thing you do (five words; not *I'd love to…*; the verb is not *begin*)

mistake.wrong: I'd like to start with explaining the background.
mistake.right: I'd like to start by explaining the background.
mistake.why: Before an *-ing* action, natives normally say *start by*; *start with* usually takes a noun (*start with some background*).

entries.related: *let me begin with* — similar, slightly more formal; *first of all* — simpler; *to kick things off* — informal.

entries.label: discourse marker
entries.meaning: Introduces a short restatement of the main points at the end of a talk, section or paper.
entries.usage: Common at the end of talks, papers and reports; on a slide it often appears as the title *Summary*. Keep what follows short: two or three points, not a new result. *To sum up* is more spoken, and *in conclusion* sounds formal and final, a bit like a school essay.
examples: So, **in summary**: the drug works, it's cheap, and side effects are rare.
**In summary**, we found no difference between the two teaching methods.
**In summary**, the roof will need to be replaced in the next two years, but the foundation is solid.

drill.sentence: {{In summary}}, we cut costs by ten percent and kept every customer. Any questions?
drill.hint: a short recap of the main points follows (two words starting with *In*; not *In short*, *In sum*, *In brief*, *In closing* or *In conclusion*)

mistake.wrong: Summarizing, our method is faster and uses less memory.
mistake.right: In summary, our method is faster and uses less memory.
mistake.why: *Summarizing,* and *Concluding,* at the start of a sentence copy German *Zusammenfassend* and *Abschließend*; English uses *In summary*, *To sum up* or *In conclusion*.

entries.related: *to sum up* — more spoken; *in conclusion* — formal, final; *in short* — very brief, often one sentence.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Invites the audience to look at or examine something together, such as a slide, graph or example.
entries.usage: Very common in talks, lectures, tutorials and meetings when you move to new content: *Let's take a look at the results*. It sounds friendly and includes the audience; *let's have a look* is more British. Don't use it before every slide; vary it with *here you can see* or *this slide shows*.
entries.pattern: let's take a (quick / closer) look at + noun / how…
examples: Now **let's take a look at** how the model behaves on noisy data.
**Let's take a look at** last quarter's numbers before we talk about hiring.
**Let's take a look at** that knee — does it hurt when I press here?

drill.sentence: Okay, enough theory. {{Let's take a look at}} a real example from one of our clinics.
drill.hint: invites the audience to examine something together (five words; the verb is not *have* or *check out*)

entries.related: *let's have a look at* — same, more British; *let's turn to* — move to a new topic; *take a closer look* — examine in more detail.

entries.term: that brings me to the end (of my talk)
entries.spoken_term: that brings me to the end of my talk
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A standard sentence that tells the audience the talk is finished, usually just before you thank them and invite questions.
entries.usage: Used at the end of talks and presentations, often right after the summary slide, and usually followed by *Thank you*. It is clear and polite, if a little formulaic; a one-sentence summary of your key point just before it makes a stronger ending. In informal settings, *That's all I have* is more common.
examples: **That brings me to the end of my talk**, so I'm happy to take questions.
And **that brings us to the end of** our tour — the gift shop is just to your left.
**That brings me to the end of** the budget update; next up is Carla with the hiring plan.

drill.sentence: So those are our three main findings, and {{that brings me to the end of}} my presentation. Thank you!
drill.hint: signals that I have finished (seven words; starts with *that*, not *this*; *me*, not *us*)

mistake.wrong: With this, I am at the end of my talk.
mistake.right: That brings me to the end of my talk.
mistake.why: The first is a word-for-word copy of German *Damit bin ich am Ende*; English speakers say *That brings me to the end*.

entries.related: *that's all I have* — informal, American; *to wrap up* — informal: I'm finishing; *which brings me to* — a transition to the next point, not the end.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: On the slide that comes after the current one in a presentation.
entries.usage: Used in talks to point forward: *On the next slide, you'll see the results*. *On* is the usual preposition for slides, as for pages and screens. Use it sparingly; a question such as *So how well does it work?* often links two slides better than announcing each one.
examples: **On the next slide**, I'll show you what happens when we double the dose.
The full budget is **on the next slide**, so don't worry about the numbers yet.
**On the next slide** you'll see a map of every bike lane in the city.

drill.sentence: Hold on to that question about costs — the numbers are {{on the next slide}}.
drill.hint: location: one click forward in the deck (four words; not *following*; the preposition is not *in*)

mistake.wrong: In the next slide, you can see the error rates.
mistake.right: On the next slide, you can see the error rates.
mistake.why: English normally uses *on* for slides, as for pages and screens.

entries.related: *in the next section* — for papers; *here you can see* — for the current slide; *moving on* — signals a change of topic.

entries.term: today I'm going to talk about
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A simple, standard opening that tells the audience the topic of your talk.
entries.usage: The most common way to state your topic in talks, lectures and webinars, usually right after a greeting. It is clear but plain, so many speakers first open with a question, a story or a striking number and then state the topic. In relaxed speech, *going to* often sounds like *gonna*.
examples: **Today I'm going to talk about** how we predict floods using river sensors and satellite data.
Good morning, everyone. **Today I'm going to talk about** what makes a good first job.
**Today I'm going to talk about** something every parent worries about: screen time.

drill.sentence: Hi everyone, thanks for coming. {{Today I'm going to talk about}} how small towns can attract young families.
drill.hint: plain opening that names the topic (six words; *I*, not *we*; a future form, not *I'd like to…* or *I want to…*)

mistake.wrong: Today I'm going to present you our new results.
mistake.right: Today I'm going to talk about our new results.
mistake.why: *Present* needs *to* before the listener (*present our results to you*); *present you our results* copies German *Ihnen … vorstellen*.

entries.related: *I'll be talking about* — same, slightly softer; *my talk is about* — plain; *the focus of this talk is* — more formal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces what the current slide presents, before you explain it.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and recorded presentations: *This slide shows our results for the three cities*. Give the main point right after it, not just a description of the axes. *Here you can see…* is more conversational, and *This graph shows…* is more precise when the slide has one chart.
examples: **This slide shows** how much water an average household uses in summer and in winter.
**This slide shows** the five steps of the new hiring process.
So **this slide shows** our main result: the error drops by half.

drill.sentence: {{This slide shows}} the number of patients we treated each month last year.
drill.hint: introduces what is on the screen now (three words; the noun is the deck page itself, not *chart*, *graph* or *figure*)

entries.related: *here you can see* — more conversational; *this graph shows* — more precise; *on the next slide* — points forward.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Along the horizontal axis of a graph; the vertical one is the y-axis.
entries.usage: Standard in talks and papers when you explain a plot: *On the x-axis we have time, and on the y-axis, temperature*. Name both axes before you talk about the result. Note that *plot A against B* puts A on the y-axis and B on the x-axis.
entries.pattern: On the x-axis / y-axis, we have + quantity; X is on the x-axis
examples: **On the x-axis**, we have the year, and on the y-axis, the average price of a home.
Time is **on the x-axis**, in hours since the patient arrived at the emergency room.
Could you put the dates **on the x-axis** instead? It's easier to read that way.

drill.sentence: In this chart, age is {{on the x-axis}} and income is on the vertical axis.
drill.hint: location in a chart: the horizontal one (three words, with a letter of the alphabet)

mistake.wrong: Both axises use a log scale.
mistake.right: Both axes use a log scale.

entries.related: *y-axis* — the vertical axis; *horizontal axis* — same as the x-axis, more formal; *plot A against B* — A on the y-axis, B on the x-axis.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Refers back to something you already said or wrote, to connect it to the current point.
entries.usage: Common in talks, meetings and emails: *As I mentioned earlier, the data come from three hospitals*. It helps the audience link ideas, but in Q&A it can sound impatient, as if the person wasn't listening, so soften it (*I touched on this briefly, but…*). *Like I said* is the casual spoken version.
examples: **As I mentioned earlier**, all of these patients were over sixty-five.
**As I mentioned earlier**, the office will be closed on Monday, so packages will be delivered Tuesday.
**As I mentioned earlier**, we have two more speakers after lunch, so please be back by one.

drill.sentence: {{As I mentioned earlier}}, the survey only included people who own a car.
drill.hint: refers back to something I said briefly (four words; the verb is not *said*, *noted* or *explained*; the last word is not *before*)

entries.related: *like I said* — casual; *as noted above* — in writing; *going back to* — returns to an earlier topic.

entries.term: I'll get to that (in a minute)
entries.spoken_term: I'll get to that in a minute
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells someone that you will discuss their point soon, later in the talk or conversation.
entries.usage: Used in talks, classes and meetings when someone asks about something you plan to cover: *Good question, I'll get to that in a minute*. It is friendly, but only if you really come back to it. *I'll come back to that* and *I'll address that later* are a little more formal.
examples: Yes, the cost is important — **I'll get to that in a minute**.
Hold that thought; **I'll get to** the parking situation **in a minute**.
Good question about the control group; **I'll get to that** on slide twelve.

drill.sentence: Great question about pricing. {{I'll get to that}} in a minute, right after the demo.
drill.hint: the speaker will deal with it shortly (four words ending in *that*; not *come to*, *talk about* or *go over*)

entries.related: *I'll come back to that* — similar, slightly more formal; *hold that thought* — informal: wait with your point; *bear with me* — asks for patience.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Checks politely whether your answer satisfied the person who asked.
entries.usage: Standard at the end of an answer in Q&A sessions, classes and support calls. It is polite and gives the person a chance to follow up, but don't ask it after every short answer. *I hope that helps* is a softer alternative when you don't want a follow-up.
examples: So no, we didn't test it on children. **Does that answer your question?**
Sorry, that was a long answer — **did that answer your question?**
**Does that answer your question**, or would you like me to go through the math?

drill.sentence: So the extra cost is mostly shipping. {{Does that answer your question}}, or should I break it down further?
drill.hint: checks the asker is satisfied (five words, present tense; not *Does that help* or *Is that clear*)

mistake.wrong: Is your question answered with this?
mistake.why: Not a grammar error, but it copies German *Ist Ihre Frage damit beantwortet?* and sounds stiff; English speakers ask with the active verb.

entries.related: *I hope that helps* — softer, closes the topic; *Is that clear?* — can sound like a teacher; *Did I get that right?* — checks your understanding, not your answer.

entries.term: if I understand your question correctly
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Shows that you are checking your understanding of a question before you answer it, usually by restating it.
entries.usage: Common in Q&A sessions, interviews and meetings, especially when a question is long or unclear. It is polite, it buys you time, and restating the question helps the rest of the audience hear it. Keep the restatement short and fair, without turning it into a question you'd prefer to answer.
examples: **If I understand your question correctly**, you're asking whether the results hold for women too.
**If I understand your question correctly**, you want to know if the refund covers shipping.
Sorry, **if I understand your question correctly**, you're worried about noise from the new road?

drill.sentence: {{If I understand your question correctly}}, you're asking why we didn't use a larger sample.
drill.hint: checks my grasp of what was asked (six words, present tense, with *your*; not *If I'm hearing you right*)

entries.related: *if I'm hearing you right* — more casual; *just to make sure I understand* — similar, before restating; *could you rephrase the question?* — when you didn't understand at all.

entries.term: go back to the previous slide
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: To return to the slide that was shown just before the current one.
entries.usage: Used by speakers who need to recheck something and by audience members in Q&A: *Could you go back to the previous slide?*. *The last slide* is ambiguous, since it can also mean the final slide, so *previous* is clearer. In casual speech, *go back one slide* is also common.
examples: Sorry, let me **go back to the previous slide** for a second.
Could you **go back to the previous slide**? I didn't catch the sample size.
Can we **go back to the previous slide** with the budget? I have a question about travel.

drill.sentence: Excuse me, could you {{go back to the previous slide}}? I'd like to see that graph again.
drill.hint: request to see the earlier page of the deck again (six words; the adjective is not *last*)

entries.related: *go back one slide* — casual; *flip back* — informal; *skip ahead* — the opposite: jump forward.

entries.spoken_term: I'd like to thank someone for
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite phrase to thank people or organizations for their help, support or invitation, often at the start or end of a talk.
entries.usage: Standard in talks, speeches and award ceremonies: *I'd like to thank my co-authors for their help*. Name people specifically and keep it short; a long list of names uses up your time. In the acknowledgments of a paper, the written form is *We thank…*.
entries.pattern: I'd like to thank + person + for + noun / -ing
examples: **I'd like to thank** my two co-authors **for** running most of these experiments.
**I'd like to thank** my mother **for** teaching me to read before kindergarten.
**I'd like to thank** the nurses on the fourth floor **for** taking such good care of my father.

drill.sentence: Before I begin, {{I'd like to thank}} Dr. Patel for her support over the past three years.
drill.hint: polite way to express gratitude (four words, beginning with *I'd*; the verb is not *acknowledge*)

mistake.wrong: I'd like to thank to my supervisor for her help.
mistake.right: I'd like to thank my supervisor for her help.
mistake.why: *Thank* takes the person directly, with no *to*; the reason follows *for*.

entries.related: *I'm grateful to* — formal, written or spoken; *thanks to* — because of (*thanks to their help*); *we thank* — standard in paper acknowledgments.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The part of a talk, event or meeting where the audience asks questions and the speaker answers.
entries.usage: Used for talks, panels, book launches and town halls: *We'll have a short Q&A at the end*. It is said *Q and A*, and *session* is often dropped. Speakers usually say at the start whether they'll take questions during the talk or save them for the Q&A.
examples: We'll leave fifteen minutes at the end for **a Q&A session**.
The best part of the book launch was **the Q&A**, when readers asked about the ending.
During **the Q&A**, someone asked whether the app works offline.

drill.sentence: Please hold your questions until {{the Q&A}} at the end of the talk.
drill.hint: the part where the audience asks things (written with an ampersand)

entries.related: *open the floor* — invite questions; *a panel discussion* — several speakers discuss; *a town hall* — US meeting where employees or citizens question leaders.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces the simple core of a method, plan or argument before the details.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and meetings when you explain a method or plan: *The basic idea is that we reuse earlier results*. Follow it with one plain sentence before the details; if it needs three sentences, it isn't basic. In speech, *that* is often dropped.
examples: **The basic idea is that** each sensor only sends data when something changes.
**The basic idea is that** you pay a little every month instead of one big bill in January.
**The basic idea is**, if a patient misses two visits, a nurse calls them at home.

drill.sentence: {{The basic idea is that}} neighbors share tools instead of each buying their own.
drill.hint: introduces the simple core of the plan (five words; the adjective means *fundamental*, not *main*, *key* or *whole*)

entries.related: *in a nutshell* — very briefly; *at a high level* — describing only the main structure; *the key insight* — the central realization that makes something work.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a simpler, shorter version of an explanation, often after a technical one.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures, interviews and conversation, right after a technical explanation. *Simply put* is a shorter version. Use it to help the audience, not after something that was already simple, or it can sound condescending.
examples: **To put it simply**, the drug stops the virus from entering the cell.
**To put it simply**, we're spending more than we earn.
The math is messy, but **to put it simply**, the model learns which words tend to appear together.

drill.sentence: The contract is long and confusing, but {{to put it simply}}, you can't sublet the apartment.
drill.hint: introduces an easier version (four words; not *to sum it up*, *basically* or *…plainly*)

mistake.wrong: Simply said, the machine learns from examples.
mistake.right: Simply put, the machine learns from examples.
mistake.why: *Simply said* copies German *einfach gesagt*; English uses *simply put* or *to put it simply*.

entries.related: *simply put* — shorter version; *in plain English* — without jargon; *in a nutshell* — in a very short summary.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a step-by-step explanation of how a method, tool or process works.
entries.usage: Common in talks, demos, tutorials and product videos to signal that a clear, practical explanation is coming. Follow it with ordered steps (*first…, then…*). In a written paper, *the method works as follows* is more formal.
examples: **Here's how it works**: you upload a photo, and the app tells you the plant's name.
The new parking system is simple. **Here's how it works**.
**Here's how it works**: every night, a script copies the new files to the backup server.

drill.sentence: Our library now lends out tools. {{Here's how it works}}: you sign up online, then pick up your drill at the front desk.
drill.hint: introduces step-by-step instructions (four words with a contraction; ends with a verb meaning *functions*)

mistake.why: After *how* in a statement, English uses normal word order, not question order.

entries.related: *let me walk you through it* — friendlier, slower; *the process is as follows* — formal, written; *step by step* — one stage at a time.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To describe the main parts or points of something briefly, without going into detail.
entries.usage: Common at the start of talks, reports and meetings: *I'll start by giving an overview of the project*. It promises a short, high-level description, so keep it short. On a slide, *Overview* or *Outline* is a common title for the agenda.
entries.pattern: give (someone) a (brief / quick) overview of + topic
examples: First, I'll **give** you **a brief overview of** how the program started.
The new manager asked each team to **give an overview of** its current projects.
Our tour guide **gave** us **a quick overview of** the city's history before we set off.

drill.sentence: Let me give you {{an overview of}} the new insurance plan before we discuss costs.
drill.hint: short description of all the main parts (three words; not *a summary of*, *a rundown of*, *a breakdown of* or *an outline of*)

mistake.wrong: Let me give you an overview over our current projects.
mistake.right: Let me give you an overview of our current projects.

entries.related: *an outline* — a list of the parts, often an agenda; *a summary* — the main points, usually at the end; *a deep dive* — the opposite: a detailed look.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An enthusiastic way to introduce your own work, news or results to an audience.
entries.usage: Very common in American talks, product launches, LinkedIn posts and company emails. In the US it sounds warm and positive, but some British and European listeners hear it as marketing, so in a formal academic talk *I'm happy to present* is a calmer choice. Use it for news you are really excited about.
entries.pattern: I'm / We're excited to share + noun / that…
examples: **I'm excited to share** some early results from our work on battery recycling.
**I'm excited to share** that I've accepted a position as a data scientist at a hospital in Seattle.
**We're excited to share** that the community garden will open on May first.

drill.sentence: Hi everyone! {{I'm excited to share}} that our team has won this year's city innovation award.
drill.hint: enthusiastic opener for good news (four words starting with *I'm*, not *We're*; not *happy*, *pleased*, *proud*, *thrilled* or *delighted*; the verb is not *announce*)

entries.related: *I'm pleased to announce* — more formal; *I'm happy to present* — calm, academic; *thrilled* — even more enthusiastic.

entries.term: I've divided my talk into (three) parts
entries.spoken_term: I've divided my talk into three parts
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the audience how your talk is organized, before you begin the first part.
entries.usage: Used in the first minute of longer talks and lectures, usually with an outline slide. Name the parts briefly, then use them as signposts later (*That brings me to part two*). In a short talk of ten minutes or less, an outline often wastes time.
entries.pattern: I've divided my talk / presentation into + number + parts
examples: **I've divided my talk into three parts**: the problem, our solution, and what's still missing.
**I've divided** this workshop **into two parts**, with a coffee break in between.
**I've divided my presentation into four short parts**, so feel free to stop me between them.

drill.sentence: {{I've divided my talk into}} three parts: background, results, and next steps.
drill.hint: describes the structure of what follows (five words; the verb is not *split*, *broken* or *organized*; the noun is not *presentation*)

mistake.wrong: I've divided my talk in three parts.
mistake.right: I've divided my talk into three parts.
mistake.why: The standard pattern is *divide into*; *divide in* is used mainly in *divide in half* and *divide in two*.

entries.related: *I'll cover three things* — more casual; *break down into* — split into parts; *an outline slide* — the agenda at the start.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: In the upper right part of a slide, screen, page or figure.
entries.usage: Used in talks, video calls and software instructions to guide people's eyes: *The legend is in the top-right corner*. *Upper right* means the same and is common in figure captions. Hyphenate it before a noun (*the top-right panel*).
examples: The legend is **in the top-right corner**, so you can see which color is which group.
Click the gear icon **in the top-right corner** to change your password.
**In the top-right corner** of the painting, you can just make out a small boat.

drill.sentence: To end the meeting, click the red button {{in the top-right corner}} of your screen.
drill.hint: location: diagonally opposite the bottom left (four words; not *upper*)

mistake.wrong: The legend is in the right upper corner.
mistake.right: The legend is in the upper-right corner.
mistake.why: English names the vertical position first (*upper-right*, *top-left*); German says *in der rechten oberen Ecke*.

entries.related: *upper right* — same, common in captions; *bottom-left* — the opposite corner; *in the corner of the screen* — less precise.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Explains what a line, color or symbol in a graph stands for.
entries.usage: Standard when you explain a plot in a talk or a caption. Explain the lines before the result, using the words people can see: *dashed*, *dotted*, *solid*, *shaded area*, *error bars*. Some listeners may be colorblind, so *dashed* or *solid* is often clearer than a color alone.
entries.pattern: The (red / dashed) line / Each dot represents + noun
examples: **The red line represents** the average temperature, and the gray area shows the range.
**The dashed line represents** what we'd expect if the drug had no effect.
**Each dot represents** one county, and the size of the dot shows its population.

drill.sentence: The red line {{represents}} the old pricing, and the blue line the new one.
drill.hint: tells us what it means (one verb starting with *re-*; not *shows*, *denotes* or *indicates*)

entries.related: *shows* — more general; *denotes* — formal, common in captions; *the legend* — the box that explains the symbols.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a plain explanation of what a result, number or rule means in practice.
entries.usage: Very common in talks, lectures and interviews, right after a technical result or a number. It moves from data to consequences, so the next words should be concrete. In speech, *that* is often dropped; used for every slide, the phrase starts to sound like filler.
examples: The error rate fell from ten percent to two. **What this means is that** doctors will see far fewer false alarms.
**What this means is that** your rent will go up by about fifty dollars a month.
**What this means for us is that** we need to hire before the summer.

drill.sentence: Interest rates went up again. {{What this means is that}} mortgages will cost more next year.
drill.hint: explains the practical consequence (five words with *this*, not *that*; a cleft structure; not *In other words* or *The upshot is*)

entries.related: *in other words* — rephrases the same point; *the upshot is* — informal: the main result; *this means that* — shorter, less emphatic.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the audience that the next point is important and should not be missed or misunderstood.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures, meetings and interviews, often to prevent a misunderstanding: *I want to stress that these are early results*. Use it once or twice in a talk, or it loses its force. *I'd like to emphasize that* is a slightly more formal version.
entries.pattern: I want to stress that + clause; I want to stress + noun
examples: **I want to stress that** these are early results from only one hospital.
**I want to stress that** nobody is losing their job because of this change.
**I want to stress** one thing: the trail is closed after dark, no exceptions.

drill.sentence: {{I want to stress that}} the survey was anonymous, so we can't follow up with individual people.
drill.hint: I'm emphasizing this point (five words; not *I'd like to…*; the verb is not *emphasize*, *underline* or *note*)

mistake.wrong: I want to stress on this point.
mistake.right: I want to stress this point.
mistake.why: The verb *stress* takes a direct object; *on* goes only with the noun (*put stress on*).

entries.related: *I'd like to emphasize* — a bit more formal; *let me be clear* — firmer, can sound defensive; *underscore* — same idea, formal American.

entries.term: this is where it gets interesting
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the audience that the most surprising or important part is coming next.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures, podcasts and storytelling, to build suspense before a key result or a twist. It works once per talk; used more often, it sounds like a sales trick. Make sure that what follows really is surprising.
examples: Most of this chili recipe is pretty standard. **This is where it gets interesting**: we add dark chocolate.
We followed the patients for a full year, and **this is where it gets interesting**: half of them got better without treatment.
We were halfway up the trail when the fog came in, and **that's where it got interesting**.

drill.sentence: The house looked perfect, and the price was low. But {{this is where it gets interesting}}: nobody had lived there for twenty years.
drill.hint: build-up before the surprising part (six words starting with *this*; the last word is not *exciting*, *weird* or *tricky*)

entries.related: *here's the twist* — introduces a surprise; *the plot thickens* — humorous; *now for the fun part* — informal.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces information that some of the audience probably already knows, without assuming that everyone does.
entries.usage: Useful in talks, emails and meetings to give background politely: *As you may know, the building will close for repairs in June*. It informs newcomers without sounding condescending to people who already know. *As you know* assumes everyone knows; *as many of you know* is a common variant in talks.
examples: **As you may know**, the clinic will move to a new building in the spring.
**As you may know**, this is the first year the conference has been held in Mexico.
**As some of you may know**, Jenna is leaving us at the end of the month.

drill.sentence: {{As you may know}}, the library is now open on Sundays from noon to five.
drill.hint: politely introduces something the audience might already be aware of (four words with a modal; the modal is not *might*)

entries.related: *as you know* — assumes everyone knows; *as many of you know* — common in talks; *you may not know this, but* — introduces a surprising fact.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Raises the question the audience is probably asking themselves, so that you can answer it.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and videos to answer a question before anyone asks it: *You may be wondering why we didn't use a larger sample*. It keeps listeners engaged and shows that you understand their concerns. In this indirect question, use statement word order after *why*: *why this matters*, not *why does this matter*.
examples: **You may be wondering why** we tested this on fruit flies instead of mice.
**You may be wondering why** the meeting starts so early. There's a good reason.
**You might be wondering** what happened to the money we raised last year.

drill.sentence: {{You may be wondering why}} we chose a small town for the pilot rather than a big city.
drill.hint: raises the question the audience is probably asking (five words; the modal is not *might*)

mistake.wrong: You may be wondering why did we use mice.
mistake.right: You may be wondering why we used mice.
mistake.why: After *wondering why*, the question is indirect, so it takes statement word order with no *did*.

entries.related: *you might ask* — similar; *the obvious question is* — more direct; *why does this matter?* — a rhetorical question to the audience.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: Asks the audience a question to involve them, usually answered by raising hands.
entries.usage: A common opener in talks, lectures and workshops: *How many of you have flown this year?*. Ask something people can answer quickly with a show of hands, and add *Raise your hand if…* to make the instruction clear. React to the result, or the question feels like a gimmick.
examples: **How many of you** have used a chatbot to write an email this week?
Quick show of hands: **how many of you** drove here today?
**How many of you** have ever lost a whole day of work to a computer crash?

drill.sentence: Let's start with a quick question. {{How many of you}} have ever moved to a new country?
drill.hint: asks the audience for a show of hands (four words, addressing them directly; not *Who here has*)

entries.related: *raise your hand if* — a clearer instruction; *who here has* — more casual; *a show of hands* — the response itself.

entries.spoken_term: to give you an idea of
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a comparison or example that helps the audience understand how big, fast or difficult something is.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and interviews before a comparison with something familiar: *To give you an idea of the scale, that's three football fields*. It works best with a concrete, everyday comparison. With *of*, it names what you are describing; without it, it introduces a whole sentence (*To give you an idea, …*).
examples: **To give you an idea of** the scale, the archive would fill about a million DVDs.
**To give you an idea of** how busy we are, we answered four thousand calls last week.
**To give you an idea**, the old roof was put on before I was born.

drill.sentence: {{To give you an idea of}} how small these particles are, a thousand of them side by side would be as wide as a human hair.
drill.hint: introduces a comparison that shows the size (six words; not *To put this in perspective* or *…a sense of*)

entries.related: *to put this in perspective* — gives a comparison that shows the real size; *for context* — background information; *for example* — a single case.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: An informal way to say you have finished your talk, update or list of points.
entries.usage: Common in American meetings, stand-ups, lab meetings and short talks. It is relaxed and brief, so it fits internal meetings better than a conference keynote. It often hands over to questions or to the next speaker: *That's all I have — any questions?*
examples: **That's all I have** for today. Any questions?
**That's all I have** for announcements, so enjoy the long weekend, everyone.
Okay, **that's all I have**; Maria, do you want to give the sales update?

drill.sentence: Those are my three updates for the week, so {{that's all I have}}. Back to you, Dave.
drill.hint: informal way to say my update is finished (four words; no *got*; not *I'm done* or *…it from me*)

entries.related: *that's it from me* — similar, informal; *I'll stop there* — polite, a bit more formal; *that brings me to the end* — standard in formal talks.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite closing sentence at the end of a talk or presentation.
entries.usage: Common at the end of formal talks, especially at international conferences, and often written on the last slide. Many American speakers prefer a shorter *Thank you* or *Thanks for listening*, followed by *I'm happy to take questions*. A final slide with your key message or contact details is usually more useful than one that only says thank you.
examples: That's the end of my presentation. **Thank you for your attention**.
**Thank you for your attention**, and I'd be happy to answer any questions.
On behalf of the whole team, **thank you for your attention** this afternoon.

drill.sentence: And with that, I'll stop here. {{Thank you for your attention}}, and enjoy the rest of the conference.
drill.hint: formal closing thanks to the audience (five words; the last word is not *time* or *patience*)

entries.related: *thanks for listening* — less formal; *thank you for your time* — common in interviews and meetings; *I'm happy to take questions* — invites the Q&A.

entries.label: polite request
entries.meaning: Politely asks someone to ask their question again in different words, because you did not understand it.
entries.usage: Useful in Q&A sessions, interviews and calls when a question is unclear, long or full of jargon. It is polite and puts no blame on the person asking. If you simply didn't hear it, ask *Could you repeat the question?* instead.
examples: Sorry, I'm not sure I follow. **Could you rephrase the question?**
**Could you rephrase the question?** I want to make sure I answer the right thing.
The interviewer's question confused me, so I asked if she **could rephrase** it.

drill.sentence: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand. {{Could you rephrase}} the question?
drill.hint: politely ask for it in different words (three words; *Could*, not *Can*; the verb is not *repeat*, *reword* or *clarify*)

mistake.why: Not wrong, but *reformulate* sounds technical in conversation and often comes from German *umformulieren*; *rephrase* is the everyday word.

entries.related: *could you repeat the question?* — when you didn't hear it; *what do you mean by…?* — asks about one word; *could you clarify?* — asks for more detail.

entries.term: that's outside my area of expertise
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A polite, honest way to say you cannot answer a question with authority because it is not your field.
entries.usage: Useful in Q&A sessions, interviews and meetings when a question goes beyond your field. It sounds honest and professional, especially if you add what you *can* say or who might know. Don't overuse it to dodge hard questions inside your own topic.
examples: **That's outside my area of expertise**, but I can put you in touch with our tax lawyer.
Honestly, **that's outside my area of expertise** — I'm a chemist, not a doctor.
The legal side **is outside my area of expertise**, so I'd rather not guess.

drill.sentence: Good question, but {{that's outside my area of expertise}}; you might ask Dr. Okafor after the session.
drill.hint: polite admission that the topic isn't yours (six words; the preposition is not *beyond*; the noun after *my* is not *field*; no *not*)

entries.related: *that's not my field* — shorter, plainer; *I'm not the best person to answer that* — polite redirect; *I'd be speculating* — admits that an answer would be a guess.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says that your team is currently investigating a question but does not have an answer yet.
entries.usage: Very common in Q&A sessions, meetings and press briefings when you have no result yet. It is honest only if you really are studying the question; otherwise listeners hear it as a polite way to avoid it. If you haven't started, *We haven't looked at that yet* is the honest answer.
examples: Whether the effect lasts longer than a year — **that's something we're looking into**.
Good point about older patients; **that's something we're looking into** right now.
Asked about the noise from the new stadium, a city spokesperson said, "**That's something we're looking into**."

drill.sentence: Will the app work without internet? {{That's something we're looking into}}, but we don't have an answer yet.
drill.hint: our team is investigating it at the moment (five words, two contractions; not *working on*)

entries.related: *look into* — investigate; *we're working on it* — trying to fix something; *we haven't looked at that* — an honest admission that you haven't studied it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Signals that you are now giving the direct answer, often after some background or a detour.
entries.usage: Common in Q&A sessions, interviews and meetings, especially after some background: *So, to answer your question: yes, it works on older phones*. It promises the direct answer now, so give it right away. *To answer your question directly* adds emphasis, and *the short answer is* works for a one-line answer.
examples: So, **to answer your question**: no, we didn't see the same effect in older adults.
**To answer your question**, the bus runs every twenty minutes on weekends.
There's a lot of history here, but **to answer your question**, yes, we're keeping the old office.

drill.sentence: That's a long story, but {{to answer your question}}, the store will reopen in March.
drill.hint: now giving the direct reply (four words; not *in short* or *long story short*)

entries.related: *in short* — for a one-line answer; *the short answer is* — gives a simple answer before the details; *to be honest* — signals frankness, not directness.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the audience you will cover this part briefly, without the details.
entries.usage: Common in talks and meetings when time is short or a slide is only background. Then really go fast; speakers who say it and then spend five minutes on the slide lose the audience's trust. *I'll just run through this* and *I'll skim over this* are close variants.
examples: This is standard background, so **I'll go through this quickly**.
**I'll go through this** part **quickly**, since most of you were at last week's meeting.
The safety rules haven't changed, so **I'll go through them quickly**.

drill.sentence: We're running out of time, so {{I'll go through this quickly}} and save the details for the handout.
drill.hint: the speaker will cover it briefly (five words with a contraction; not *run…*, *skim…* or *go over*)

entries.related: *run through* — go over quickly; *skim over* — mention without detail; *I'll spare you the details* — skip the details entirely.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Promises the audience that you will speak only for a short time.
entries.usage: Common at the start of short speeches, toasts, announcements and meeting updates: *I'll keep this brief, because I know you're hungry*. It is polite and sets expectations, but only say it if you mean it. *I'll keep it short* is slightly more casual; *I'll be brief* is more formal.
examples: **I'll keep this brief** — I know everyone wants to get to lunch.
Thanks for coming, everyone. **I'll keep this brief**: the move is on Friday, and the movers come at eight.
At the wedding, my brother promised to **keep it brief** and then spoke for twenty minutes.

drill.sentence: I know it's late, so {{I'll keep this brief}}: the project is on schedule and under budget.
drill.hint: the speaker promises to be short (four words with a contraction; *this*, not *it*; the adjective is not *short*)

entries.related: *I'll be brief* — more formal; *I'll keep it short* — casual; *long story short* — summarizes a story quickly.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces an example, picture or demonstration that makes a point clearer.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and essays, right after an abstract claim: *To illustrate this, let's look at two patients*. Follow it immediately with a concrete case, picture or demo. In writing, *For example* or *Consider…* is often shorter.
examples: **To illustrate this**, let's look at two patients with the same symptoms but different outcomes.
Small changes add up. **To illustrate this**, imagine saving five dollars a day for ten years.
**To illustrate this point**, I brought two of the old phones with me.

drill.sentence: Language changes fast online. {{To illustrate this}}, here are five words that didn't exist ten years ago.
drill.hint: introduces an example that makes the point clear (three words ending in *this*; the verb is not *show* or *demonstrate*)

entries.related: *for example* — introduces one case; *to make this concrete* — turns an abstract idea into a specific case; *case in point* — informal: here is an example that proves it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a last point about the current topic before you change to the next one.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and meetings to add a last remark or check for questions: *Before I move on, are there any questions about this part?*. It helps listeners notice that the topic is about to change. *Before we move on* includes the audience and sounds a bit warmer.
examples: **Before I move on**, are there any questions about the sampling method?
**Before I move on**, I should say that these numbers don't include part-time staff.
**Before we move on** to dessert, I'd like to say a few words about Grandma.

drill.sentence: {{Before I move on}}, I want to point out one problem with this graph.
drill.hint: signals a last remark on the current topic (four words; *I*, not *we*; the verb is not *continue* or *go on*)

entries.related: *moving on* — signals the change itself; *one more thing* — introduces a final point; *before we wrap up* — near the end of a meeting.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Introduces a specific example that shows what an abstract idea means in practice.
entries.usage: Common in technical talks, lectures and papers, right after a general statement or a formula: *To make this concrete, suppose we have three servers*. Give real numbers or a real case. *To make this more concrete* and *concretely* are common variants.
examples: **To make this concrete**, suppose a patient takes the pill every morning but skips weekends.
**To make this concrete**, imagine a family of four with one car and two jobs across town.
**To make this more concrete**, here's what the error looks like on a real photo.

drill.sentence: Inflation slowly eats your savings. {{To make this concrete}}, at three percent a year, a hundred dollars loses about a quarter of its value in ten years.
drill.hint: introduces a specific example of an abstract idea (four words; *this*, not *it*; not *For example* or *To illustrate*)

entries.related: *to illustrate this* — introduces an example or a picture; *concretely* — one word, same idea; *in the abstract* — the opposite: in general terms.

entries.label: spoken question
entries.meaning: A rhetorical question that introduces the explanation of why a result or topic is important.
entries.usage: Very common in talks, lectures and science communication, after a technical result and before the take-home message. You ask it and answer it yourself, so pause briefly after it. Once or twice it keeps a talk focused on impact; on every slide it becomes a habit the audience notices.
examples: Our sensor costs two dollars instead of two hundred. **Why does this matter?** Because small rural clinics can afford it.
Bees are disappearing in some regions. So **why does this matter** for your grocery bill?
**Why does this matter?** Because one in five adults in the city doesn't have a car.

drill.sentence: This new battery charges in five minutes. {{Why does this matter}}? Because it makes electric trucks practical for long routes.
drill.hint: rhetorical question about importance (four words with *this*; not *Why is this important* or *Why should we care*)

mistake.wrong: Why this matters? Because it saves hospitals money.
mistake.right: Why does this matter? Because it saves hospitals money.
mistake.why: A direct question needs *does* and question word order; *why this matters* is not a question and works only as a heading or inside a sentence (*here's why this matters*).

entries.related: *so what?* — informal, can sound blunt; *why should we care?* — more casual; *the big picture* — the wider importance.

entries.term: we have time for one more question
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said by a session chair or speaker to allow only one final question before the session ends.
entries.usage: Standard for chairs and moderators at conferences, panels and town halls when time is running out. It is a polite, clear signal, and speakers often add *…but I'm happy to talk afterward*. *We're out of time* ends the questions completely.
examples: **We have time for one more question** — yes, the woman in the back.
I'm afraid **we only have time for one more question** before the coffee break.
**We have time for one more question**, and then the author has to catch her flight.

drill.sentence: We're almost out of time, so {{we have time for one more question}}. Yes, you in the front.
drill.hint: the chair allows only one final asker (seven words; no *got*; the adjective is not *last*)

entries.related: *let's take one last question* — same, from the speaker; *we're out of time* — no more questions; *I'm happy to talk afterward* — invites people to ask later.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A host's formal phrase to introduce a speaker and invite the audience to applaud.
entries.usage: Used by hosts and chairs at the end of an introduction, just before the speaker walks up: *Please join me in welcoming Dr. Sarah Kim*. It tells the audience to applaud. It is standard at conferences, award ceremonies, company events and graduations.
examples: **Please join me in welcoming** our keynote speaker, Dr. Maria Lopez.
Without further ado, **please join me in welcoming** this year's graduating class.
**Please join me in welcoming** Tom, who's moving to our design team from the Chicago office.

drill.sentence: She has written four books on ocean science, so {{please join me in welcoming}} Professor Ana Ruiz.
drill.hint: invites applause for the next speaker (five words; not *put your hands together for* or *give a warm welcome to*)

entries.related: *put your hands together for* — informal, very energetic; *without further ado* — introduces the main event; *it's my pleasure to introduce* — formal start of an introduction.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Approximately, or in a simplified way that ignores some details.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and technical conversations, both for rough numbers (*roughly speaking, half the users*) and for simplified explanations (*roughly speaking, the model guesses the next word*). It warns listeners that the statement is not exact. In papers, *approximately* is more usual for numbers and *informally* for simplified explanations.
examples: **Roughly speaking**, a third of our budget goes to rent.
**Roughly speaking**, the algorithm keeps the parts of the image that change the most.
**Roughly speaking**, it's a two-hour drive to the coast if there's no traffic.

drill.sentence: {{Roughly speaking}}, the Earth is four times as wide as the Moon.
drill.hint: signals a rough, not exact, statement (two words; not *more or less*, *broadly…* or *loosely…*)

entries.related: *approximately* — more formal, for numbers; *broadly speaking* — in general terms, about ideas; *more or less* — informal: nearly.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Says you will skip the boring, complicated or unpleasant details and give only the main point.
entries.usage: Common in talks, meetings and storytelling, often with light humor: *I'll spare you the details, but it took three months to fix*. In a talk it signals that the details don't matter for this audience; *the details are in the paper* is the more formal version. *I'll spare you the gory details* is a humorous variant for unpleasant stories.
examples: The proof is long, so **I'll spare you the details** and just show the result.
We had a disaster with the movers — **I'll spare you the details**.
**I'll spare you the gory details**, but the surgery went fine and I'm home now.

drill.sentence: Getting the permit took four visits to city hall, but {{I'll spare you the details}}.
drill.hint: skip the boring parts for your sake (five words with a contraction; the verb is not *skip* or *save*)

entries.related: *long story short* — summarizes quickly; *the gory details* — humorous: all the unpleasant details; *the details are in the paper* — formal pointer to the full version.

entries.term: the details are in the paper
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the audience that the full technical details are in the written paper, not in the talk.
entries.usage: Standard in conference talks and seminars, to keep the talk short: *I'll skip the proof; the details are in the paper*. It is fine for derivations and side experiments, but not as an answer to a basic question in Q&A. Put the paper's title or a QR code on the slide so people can find it.
examples: I'll skip the derivation, but **the details are in the paper**.
We tried six other settings as well — **the details are in the paper**, in Section 5.
**The full details are in the report**, which we'll share with all of you after the meeting.

drill.sentence: We tested twelve other ways to clean the data; {{the details are in the paper}} if you're interested.
drill.hint: you can read the full version in the publication (five words starting with *the*; the last word is not *appendix*)

entries.related: *see the appendix* — written pointer; *I'll spare you the details* — informal; *happy to discuss offline* — after the talk.

entries.term: thank you for the kind introduction
entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: The polite first words of a speaker after a host has introduced them.
entries.usage: Standard at conferences, seminars, award events and invited talks; say it right after you reach the podium, often with the host's name: *Thank you, Maria, for the kind introduction*. Keep it to one sentence before you start your talk. *Thanks for that kind introduction* is a little warmer and less formal.
examples: **Thank you for the kind introduction**, and thank you all for coming.
**Thank you, Dr. Chen, for the kind introduction** — I'm honored to be here.
**Thanks for that kind introduction** — I'm not sure I deserve all of it.

drill.sentence: {{Thank you for the kind introduction}}, John. It's a real pleasure to be back in Boston.
drill.hint: first polite words after the host presents you (six words; *the*, not *that*; the adjective is not *generous* or *warm*)

entries.related: *thank you for having me* — thanks the organizers for the invitation; *please join me in welcoming* — the host's line; *it's a pleasure to be here* — a common next sentence.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Points forward to something that the talk or text will show later.
entries.usage: Common in talks, lectures and textbooks to tell the audience that a point will matter later: *As we'll see later, this choice turns out to be important*. It builds anticipation, but only if you really come back to it. In writing, *as we will see in Section 4* is more precise.
examples: This small detail, **as we'll see later**, explains most of the error.
**As we'll see later**, the cheaper option actually costs more over five years.
**As we'll see** in the second half of the course, these two ideas are closely related.

drill.sentence: {{As we'll see later}}, the first owners of this house left a few surprises in the basement.
drill.hint: points forward to a part still to come (four words, subject *we*; the verb is not *show* or *discuss*)

entries.related: *as I mentioned earlier* — points back; *more on this later* — informal; *I'll come back to this* — promises to return to a point.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: If there is enough time; used for extra items that you will cover only if the schedule allows.
entries.usage: Common in talk outlines, meeting agendas and course plans, for items you may have to skip: *If time permits, I'll show a short demo*. It sounds polite and a little formal, and it lowers expectations for that item. *If we have time* is the everyday version, and *time permitting* is a shorter formal variant.
examples: **If time permits**, I'll end with a short demo of the app.
**If time permits**, the class will also cover how to write a strong cover letter.
**Time permitting**, we'll also discuss next year's budget.

drill.sentence: The tour covers the main gallery and, {{if time permits}}, the sculpture garden.
drill.hint: condition: enough minutes remain (three words, formal; the verb is not *allows*)

mistake.wrong: If the time permits, we'll look at a second example.
mistake.right: If time permits, we'll look at a second example.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase has no article; *if the time permits* copies German *wenn die Zeit es erlaubt*.

entries.related: *time permitting* — same, shorter; *if we have time* — casual; *if possible* — more general.
